Heparin- coated stents have been used to reduce periprocedural thrombosis and may reduce long-term stenosis,50 but stents releasing antiproliferative drugs are most widely used. Both sirolimus- and paclitaxel-eluting stents have been shown75,76 to reduce neointimal proliferation and clinical events, including the need for repeat revascularisation, and they appear to be more effective than intravascular brachy- therapy.77,78 Outcomes may be better with sirolimus than with paclitaxel,79 but this does not appear to be clinically important.80,81 Other drugs that are used include sirolimus analogues such as everolimus and zotarolimus, and dexa- methasone; lanreotide, and the sirolimus analogues tac- rolimus and biolimus A9 are under investigation. Use of a paclitaxel-coated angioplasty balloon has also been tried,82 and local gene therapy is also under investigation. Although drug-eluting stents clearly reduce the incidence of restenosis, late stent thrombosis has been reported83,84 and appears to occur more frequently than with bare-metal stents;85 possible mechanisms include delayed endotheli- alisation due to the drug or hypersensitivity reactions pos- sibly related to the polymer coating.86 However, analyses using different definitions of late thrombosis have suggested87 that there is no significant difference between the types of stent, and the clinical relevance of any increase in the incidence of late thrombosis remains unclear. The effect of drug-eluting stents on mortality has also been de- bated; some analyses88,89 have reported an increased mor- tality with drug-eluting stents, whereas others85,90 have found no significant effect. There is some evidence91,92 that outcomes with drug-eluting stents are worse in high- risk clinical situations, although observational studies93,94 suggest they are as safe as bare metal stents in such pa- tients, and it appears that late events may be related to du- ration of antiplatelet therapy.84 The FDA has stated46 that the concerns about thrombosis do not outweigh the bene- fits of drug-eluting stents when used for their approved in- dications, but that outcomes may not be the same in other patients. 1.
